paragraphs: BSemiFL addresses how clients should assign training labels to their unlabeled data when learning a shared model together. Each client has access to a local model and a global model informed by other clients. Choosing which model to trust matters because these models bring different kinds of knowledge to the same sample.

The paper’s theoretical and empirical analysis finds that local models label their own data more accurately, while the global model can progressively improve labeling by contributing knowledge from other clients. BSemiFL turns this complementary relationship into a sample-specific decision. Bayesian inference estimates how closely each model relates to a particular sample, and those estimates determine the weights used to combine their proposed labels.

The theoretical analysis establishes lower labeling error than using either model alone or averaging them equally. Experiments report performance improvements of up to 9.8% over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a principled way to balance local familiarity with shared knowledge during the labeling step that supports subsequent collaborative training.
icml-2025-bsemifl-semi-supervised-federa.tldr: BSemiFL uses Bayesian, sample-specific weighting of local and global predictions to improve labels for semi-supervised federated learning.

paragraphs: CSG-ODE models graphs whose node states and relationships change over time. Existing graph neural differential-equation models combine uncertain latent representations with continuous evolution, but the paper identifies difficulties with changing connections and nonlinear node behavior. Its approach modifies both the encoding of graph histories and the prediction of their future evolution.

During encoding, the model estimates the importance of interactions between nodes through information transmission. It combines these importance weights with latent correlations to guide an adaptive graph convolutional recurrent network, producing temporal node representations. During decoding, differential equations describe how node states evolve, with nonlinear subnetworks supplying the flexibility needed to represent more complex changes.

For tasks that require stability, the authors introduce SCSG-ODE, which constrains weight matrices to learnable anti-symmetric forms and provides a theoretical stability guarantee. Experiments cover traffic, motion capture, and simulated physical systems. The authors report that CSG-ODE outperforms state-of-the-art graph differential-equation models, while the stable variant delivers superior performance and the strongest reported stability in those evaluations.
icml-2025-csg-ode-controlsynth-graph-ode.tldr: CSG-ODE models changing graph relationships and nonlinear node dynamics, with a constrained variant that provides enhanced stability.

paragraphs: SPACY seeks causal relationships in measurements arranged across space and time, such as climate grids. These data are challenging because there may be many grid points, and nearby locations often carry correlated information. The framework discovers latent time series and studies causal connections among them, reducing the dimensionality of the causal discovery problem.

The method uses variational inference and spatial factors defined by kernel functions. These factors connect observed grid measurements to latent representations, allowing spatially related observations to be aggregated. For its theoretical analysis, the paper extends the setting to continuous space. It establishes identifiability when observations come from a nonlinear, invertible function of the product of latent series and spatial factors.

That result avoids additional assumptions about instantaneous effects or sufficient variability that the authors describe as often unverifiable. Experiments show stronger performance than state-of-the-art baselines on synthetic data, including difficult settings, while supporting large grids. On climate data, SPACY recovers known phenomena, providing evidence that the latent representation can capture scientifically meaningful structure.
icml-2025-discovering-latent-causal-grap.tldr: SPACY discovers causal relationships among latent time series extracted from spatial grids, with an identifiability result under a specified observation model.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision policies that remain effective when the relationship between observed features and outcomes changes. Its setting is concept drift: the conditional outcome distribution changes while the covariate distribution stays fixed. Modeling this specific source of change can avoid the unnecessary conservatism of protecting against changes to the entire joint distribution.

The authors first construct a doubly robust estimator of a policy’s worst-case average reward over a set of perturbed conditional distributions. They establish asymptotic normality even when nuisance quantities are estimated more slowly than the root-sample-size rate. The learning algorithm then selects the policy with the highest estimated robust value from a specified policy class.

The theoretical suboptimality bound scales as a policy-class complexity measure divided by the square root of sample size. A matching lower bound establishes the optimality of this rate. Numerical studies report substantial improvements over existing benchmarks. Together, these results support tailoring robustness to the assumed form of drift, with both statistical guarantees and empirical evidence for the resulting policies.
icml-2025-distributionally-robust-policy.tldr: The paper learns robust policies for changes in conditional outcomes, achieving an optimal statistical rate and improved numerical performance.

paragraphs: Graph prompting adapts a pretrained graph model by learning additional tokens or subgraphs attached to its input. This lets the model serve new applications without retraining its pretrained parameters. Although this approach has shown empirical success, the paper asks what theoretical guarantees explain its ability to reproduce useful operations on graph data.

The authors develop a framework that interprets prompts as approximations to graph transformation operators. A formal theorem establishes their capacity to approximate these transformations, connecting the tasks used before and after adaptation. The analysis also provides upper bounds on approximation error for an individual graph and extends the discussion to batches of graphs.

The paper then studies how data-operation errors are distributed, extending the theoretical treatment from linear graph models to nonlinear ones. Experiments support the analysis and its practical implications. The contribution is an account of what graph prompting can approximate and how its error can be bounded, giving mathematical substance to a technique previously supported largely by experimental results.
icml-2025-does-graph-prompt-work-a-data-.tldr: The paper explains graph prompting through guarantees that prompts can approximate graph transformations, together with bounds and analyses of approximation error.

paragraphs: DynaMind addresses how an embodied agent can connect a short language instruction to the much richer information contained in video. Its central idea is to extract a compact description of important visual content and how it changes over time. This dynamic representation becomes the basis for reasoning about what to do next.

The framework uses an adaptive component called FrameScorer to assign importance scores to video frames. Scores reflect semantic consistency and visual saliency, helping identify relevant content while filtering redundancy. The selected information is combined into compact representations that retain key spatial and temporal patterns, making the video more directly usable for decision-making.

DynaMind then predicts critical future dynamics and uses a policy guided by those dynamics to generate coherent, context-sensitive actions. Across several simulation benchmarks and real-world scenarios, the authors report significant improvements over the evaluated baselines. These findings support the usefulness of connecting video selection, anticipation, and action through a shared representation of change.
icml-2025-dynamind-reasoning-over-abstra.tldr: DynaMind condenses video into important dynamics, predicts relevant future changes, and uses them to guide embodied actions.

paragraphs: This paper improves protein representation learning by changing how alternative views of a protein graph are constructed for contrastive learning. Existing approaches described in the abstract modify two-dimensional graph topology without sufficiently accounting for biological properties or three-dimensional structure. The proposed approach creates varied views while aiming to preserve important protein characteristics.

The first strategy preserves functional communities within the graph. It uses spectral constraints to retain community structure and weights edges according to chemical similarity between residues, guiding which edges are sampled. The second strategy operates on three-dimensional protein structure, perturbing dihedral angles and rotating secondary structures while retaining critical structural information.

Both strategies are integrated into a protein graph contrastive-learning framework. Their shared principle is invariance: useful variation should leave important properties intact, giving the learner more informative views of the same protein. Experiments across four protein-related tasks show superior performance for the proposed framework. The results support incorporating biological and structural knowledge into the augmentation process used to learn protein representations.
icml-2025-enhancing-graph-contrastive-le.tldr: Biology-aware graph augmentations preserve functional communities and critical three-dimensional structure to improve contrastive protein representation learning.

paragraphs: Fed-ICL addresses a bottleneck in question answering with in-context learning: good examples may be distributed across client devices instead of being readily available in one place. Privacy constraints, annotation costs, and differences between data distributions can make suitable examples scarce. The paper explores how clients can collaboratively improve answers using their local resources.

The framework organizes multiple rounds of interaction between clients and a central server. Answers are progressively refined through this collaborative process, allowing local datasets to contribute to response quality. Because it does not require transmitting model parameters, Fed-ICL avoids the parameter-transfer burden identified in existing approaches while retaining the parameter-free adaptation characteristic of in-context learning.

The authors establish theoretical convergence guarantees and evaluate the framework on standard question-answering benchmarks. Their experiments show strong answer quality alongside low communication costs. The contribution is an iterative mechanism for using distributed examples effectively, connecting collaborative answer refinement with a theoretical account of convergence and practical evidence that communication can remain inexpensive.
icml-2025-federated-in-context-learning-.tldr: Fed-ICL improves question-answering responses through repeated client–server refinement using local data without transmitting model parameters.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces translate neural activity into behavioral actions, but neural signals change across days. A decoder trained on one day can therefore work less well later. Aligning signals between days can help, yet the paper identifies instability and poor performance when only a few trials are available to perform that alignment.

The authors introduce Flow-Based Distribution Alignment, or FDA, to make adaptation effective with very little new data. It uses flow matching to learn flexible neural representations whose latent dynamics are stable. These representations support source-free alignment through likelihood maximization, allowing adaptation without requiring source data during the alignment process.

The paper proves stability of the latent dynamics using Lyapunov exponents and evaluates the framework across multiple motor cortex datasets. Experiments report superior performance and reliable adaptation with fewer than five trials. The theoretical result addresses stability, while the experiments show practical few-trial performance. Together, they suggest a route toward reducing the recalibration burden that limits the long-term usefulness of brain-computer interfaces.
icml-2025-flow-matching-for-few-trial-ne.tldr: FDA uses flow matching with provably stable latent dynamics to adapt neural decoders, reporting reliable results with fewer than five trials.

paragraphs: GraphCL tackles medical image segmentation when labeled examples are limited and unlabeled images must contribute to learning. The paper argues that previous semi-supervised approaches have emphasized increasingly complex training strategies while overlooking structural relationships in the data. Its proposal is to model those relationships explicitly within a unified deep-learning system.

The method introduces graph-based clustering into segmentation learning. It combines raw features with pairwise affinities between local image features, giving the model both information about individual features and information about how they relate. These inputs support clustered features across different graphs. This makes data structure part of the learned representation used for segmentation.

The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first explicit modeling of data-structure information for this semi-supervised medical segmentation setting. On three standard benchmarks, GraphCL outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods. The findings support the value of adding relational structure to the learning process when annotations are scarce, alongside the broader goal of making more effective use of unlabeled medical images.
icml-2025-graphcl-graph-based-clustering.tldr: GraphCL combines local image features and their pairwise relationships through graph-based clustering to improve semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

paragraphs: Griffin explores a foundation-model approach to relational databases, aiming to support diverse prediction tasks through shared machinery. The paper contrasts this with smaller models trained for individual database tasks. Its design unifies data encoding and task decoding so that pretraining can contribute to multiple datasets and uses.

The model is pretrained on both single-table data and relational databases. It includes encoders for categorical, numerical, and metadata features, together with cross-attention, a new aggregation component, and enhanced message-passing networks. These components let the model process different feature types and the connections represented by graphs extracted from relational data.

Evaluation spans large, heterogeneous, and temporal database graphs across several domains, collectively exceeding 150 million nodes. Griffin performs better than or comparably to individually trained models and is particularly effective when data are limited. The authors also report strong transfer to new datasets and tasks, with similarity and diversity in pretraining contributing to transferability. These results support Griffin’s potential as a broadly reusable relational-database model.
icml-2025-griffin-towards-a-graph-centri.tldr: Griffin shares graph-based encoding and task decoding across relational databases, showing strong transfer and performance in low-data settings.

paragraphs: This paper develops regression for multidimensional predictors and responses while preserving their tensor structure. Such data can contain correlations along several directions that vector- or matrix-based models struggle to capture. The proposed model handles high dimensionality by assuming that the relevant tensor structure occupies an unknown, lower-dimensional subspace.

The estimation approach combines least squares with nonconvex penalties that express structural properties such as sparsity and low rank. These assumptions narrow the effective complexity of the regression problem. The authors derive general bounds on estimation risk and show that, under mild technical conditions, the estimators attain oracle statistical rates, matching rates associated with knowing the relevant underlying structure.

To compute the estimators, the paper introduces an accelerated proximal-gradient algorithm and reports rapid convergence in practice. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the model’s effectiveness. The contribution connects a structured model, statistical guarantees, and a practical optimization procedure, showing how low-dimensional organization can make high-dimensional tensor regression more tractable.
icml-2025-high-dimensional-tensor-regres.tldr: Structured tensor regression with nonconvex penalties achieves oracle statistical rates under stated conditions and is paired with an efficient optimization algorithm.

paragraphs: INRFlow targets a design obstacle in generative modeling across different data types. Many flow-matching systems first train a compressor and then train a generator in the compressor’s latent space. Because different modalities use specially designed compressors, this two-stage process makes it harder to develop one approach that transfers naturally across domains.

The paper proposes training flow-matching transformers directly in the data’s ambient space. Inspired by implicit neural representations, it introduces a conditionally independent, pointwise training objective that supports predictions continuously over coordinates. This gives the model a coordinate-based way to represent data without first relying on a separately trained, modality-specific compressor.

Experiments cover images, three-dimensional point clouds, and protein structures. The authors report strong performance across these domains and improvements over comparable approaches. These results support the feasibility of a shared generative design for substantially different kinds of data. The paper presents INRFlow as a step toward domain-agnostic flow matching, with the demonstrated breadth coming from the modalities evaluated.
icml-2025-inrflow-flow-matching-for-inrs.tldr: INRFlow trains coordinate-based flow-matching transformers directly in ambient space, demonstrating strong generation across images, point clouds, and protein structures.

paragraphs: This paper examines fairness differences that correctness-based evaluation can miss. Two groups may receive similarly accurate predictions even when a language model is systematically more confident about one group. The authors argue that assessing uncertainty alongside accuracy provides a finer-grained view of bias in model decisions.

They introduce UCerf, an uncertainty-aware fairness metric, and a dataset focused on gender and occupation in co-reference resolution. The dataset contains 31,756 examples and is designed to address shortcomings in the size, diversity, and clarity of existing evaluation data. Together, the metric and dataset support comparisons that account for how certain a model is about its answers.

The evaluation covers eight open-source language models. One reported example is Mistral-8B, whose high confidence in incorrect predictions produces a fairness concern detected by UCerf but overlooked by Equalized Odds. This illustrates the paper’s central contribution: uncertainty can reveal disparities that are hidden when evaluation records only whether each answer is correct.
icml-2025-is-your-model-fairly-certain-u.tldr: UCerf combines uncertainty with fairness evaluation to expose disparities that correctness-based metrics can overlook.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a language model’s performance changes during continual pretraining, when a pretrained model receives further training on a particular domain. It tracks both general and domain-specific performance through validation loss. The goal is to understand the learning trajectory well enough to predict it and choose training settings for different objectives.

The authors observe that the loss trajectory can be understood as a transition between an initial curve and another hidden curve. Their formulation separates the effect of changing the training-data distribution from the effect of gradually reducing the learning rate. Combining these factors yields a scaling law for predicting loss across continual-training steps and learning-rate schedules.

The formulation accounts for training duration, learning rate, and the distance between the original and continual-pretraining data distributions. It can also guide hyperparameter choices when balancing general performance against domain specialization. Experiments across multiple continual-pretraining datasets and settings support the scaling law, providing empirical evidence that this decomposition captures useful regularities in adaptation.
icml-2025-learning-dynamics-in-continual.tldr: A continual-pretraining scaling law separates distribution shift from learning-rate effects to predict loss trajectories and guide training choices.

paragraphs: Autoregressive models generate data one piece at a time, making the order of those decisions part of the modeling problem. Text offers a familiar left-to-right sequence, but graphs do not provide an equally obvious canonical order. This paper makes the generation order itself a learned, probabilistic component.

The proposed model includes an order-policy: a trainable probability distribution that chooses the next generation step based on the current state. Consequently, the order can change as generation proceeds. To train this system, the authors derive a variational lower bound on exact log-likelihood and optimize it using stochastic gradient estimates.

Experiments show that the model learns meaningful orderings for both image and graph generation. For molecular graphs, the authors report state-of-the-art results on QM9 and ZINC250k using Fréchet ChemNet Distance, Synthetic Accessibility Score, and Quantitative Estimate of Drug-likeness. These findings support learning how to sequence generation decisions when the data do not come with a natural order.
icml-2025-learning-order-autoregressive-.tldr: A learned, state-dependent order-policy lets autoregressive models choose their generation sequence, with strong results on molecular graph benchmarks.

paragraphs: LightGTS explores how a general forecasting model can work efficiently across different time-series datasets. The paper identifies a cost of existing foundation-model approaches: large pretrained models can generalize well but impose substantial computational demands. Its alternative builds a lightweight model around recurring patterns already present in time series.

The first component, Periodical Tokenization, extracts consistent periodic patterns from datasets with different scales and intrinsic periods. This gives multi-source pretraining a way to handle variation while retaining recurring structure. The second component, Periodical Parallel Decoding, uses historical tokens during prediction so that periodic information also informs the decoding stage.

Together, these components make periodicity an explicit design principle for both representing the past and forecasting the future. Across nine real-world benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art forecasting performance in zero-shot and full-shot settings, with substantially better efficiency than existing time-series foundation models. The results support periodic modeling as a useful route to strong general forecasting with a smaller computational burden.
icml-2025-lightgts-a-lightweight-general.tldr: LightGTS uses periodic tokenization and decoding to deliver strong general forecasting with a lightweight, computationally efficient model.

paragraphs: LoRT addresses tensor regression when the target task has too few samples to learn effectively on its own. It transfers knowledge from related source tasks while accounting for differences between tasks. These differences can involve both the regression models and the distributions of input data, making direct reuse of source information challenging.

The framework combines a fusion regularizer with a two-step refinement procedure. Its aim is to adapt transferred knowledge robustly while preserving a low-tubal-rank tensor structure, a form of compact organization in multidimensional data. This structural requirement remains part of the learning problem as information moves between source and target tasks.

For decentralized data, the authors introduce D-LoRT, a distributed version designed to retain statistical efficiency with little communication overhead. Theory and experiments on tensor regression, including compressed sensing and completion, support the methods’ robustness and versatility. The findings indicate that structured transfer can help data-scarce tensor problems even when task differences and distributed data management complicate collaboration.
icml-2025-low-rank-tensor-transitions-lo.tldr: LoRT transfers knowledge between tensor-regression tasks while preserving low-rank structure, with a distributed variant for decentralized data.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential recommendations when users provide preferences between pairs of items. Existing clustering-of-bandits methods help multiple users learn collaboratively by grouping similar users and sharing data within groups. However, these methods typically expect numerical rewards, which may be less practical to obtain than a direct comparison between two options.

The authors introduce clustering algorithms for dueling bandits, bringing user collaboration into this preference-feedback setting. COLDB assumes that user rewards are linear functions of contextual features. CONDB uses a neural network to represent more complex, nonlinear reward functions. Both combine learning from pairwise feedback with adaptive grouping of users.

Theoretical analyses show that collaboration improves regret bounds, which measure accumulated decision loss relative to better choices. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets further support the effectiveness of the methods. The contribution is a way to share information across users while working with the kind of comparative feedback that recommendation applications may more realistically collect.
icml-2025-online-clustering-of-dueling-b.tldr: COLDB and CONDB cluster users to share information while learning sequential decisions from pairwise preferences, with improved regret bounds.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the task of retrieving the original image behind an image edited by a text-guided diffusion model. Such tracing could help address misuse involving misinformation, copyright infringement, or obscured origins. The challenge is that edits from different diffusion models can look different enough to undermine ordinary feature-similarity matching.

The authors contribute OriPID, a dataset of original images and editing prompts for training and evaluating identification across diffusion models. Their method operates on embeddings from a pretrained variational autoencoder. They prove the existence of a linear transformation that minimizes distances between generated-image embeddings and their corresponding original-image embeddings, then demonstrate that such a transformation can generalize across diffusion models.

Experiments report strong cross-model generalization and a 31.6% mAP improvement over similarity-based methods, including approaches designed for generalization. The result suggests that aligning the embedding relationship between originals and edits can be more effective for this task than relying on visual similarity learned from one diffusion model’s outputs.
icml-2025-origin-identification-for-text.tldr: A linear transformation of autoencoder embeddings helps retrieve the source images of diffusion edits and generalizes across different diffusion models.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether quantum data re-uploading models predict accurately on unseen examples. These models have attracted attention for their expressivity and trainability, but those qualities do not by themselves establish predictive performance. The study focuses on what happens when high-dimensional inputs are processed using a limited number of qubits.

The theoretical result identifies a failure mode as the number of encoding layers increases: predictive performance progressively approaches random guessing in the studied setting. Repeatedly uploading the data does not resolve this degradation. The finding therefore places a constraint on the usefulness of increasing encoding depth when the circuit has limited width.

Experiments on synthetic, linearly separable data and on real-world datasets support the theoretical analysis. Based on these results, the authors recommend wider circuit architectures for high-dimensional data instead of increasing depth in narrow circuits. The contribution is a predictive-performance perspective on architecture design, showing why greater encoding depth can be counterproductive under the conditions examined.
icml-2025-predictive-performance-of-deep.tldr: For high-dimensional data with limited qubits, deeper encoding can drive quantum re-uploading models toward random-guessing performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks why refusal-trained language models struggle with jailbreak attacks that differ from their training examples. It investigates whether the problem is a lack of safety knowledge or a failure to use knowledge already present. Best-of-N evaluations show substantial safety gains as more candidate outputs are considered, indicating that useful safety knowledge remains latent.

A domain-adaptation analysis attributes part of the problem to superficial shortcuts learned during direct refusal training. These shortcuts produce representations that do not generalize well to unfamiliar attacks. The proposed response is to train models to reason about safety for each query, using synthetic reasoning supervision aligned with specified guidelines reflecting diverse perspectives on safety knowledge.

The aim is to make relevant safety knowledge more consistently available during response generation. Extensive experiments show significant improvements in generalization against out-of-distribution attacks. The findings support a distinction between possessing safety knowledge and reliably applying it, and demonstrate that guideline-based reasoning supervision can improve that application in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-safety-reasoning-with-guidelin.tldr: Training models to reason from safety guidelines improves their ability to apply latent safety knowledge against unfamiliar jailbreak attacks.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimization method for entropy-regularized optimal transport. Although this formulation supports scalable transport-based applications, commonly used solvers can converge slowly. Methods that use second-order information offer another route, but approximating the Hessian by a sparse matrix has lacked sufficient theoretical explanation and can work poorly when the transport plan is dense.

The authors first analyze the benefits of Hessian sparsification, providing a foundation for more flexible choices of which entries to retain. They then augment the sparse approximation with a low-rank term. This additional component is designed to better represent the dense case while remaining within a quasi-Newton framework that uses an approximate Hessian.

The paper rigorously analyzes convergence and evaluates the algorithm on large-scale optimal transport problems. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved solver performance. Its contribution combines a better theoretical account of sparsification with an approximation that can capture more than sparse structure alone, directly addressing the dense-plan difficulty identified in earlier second-order approaches.
icml-2025-the-sparse-plus-low-rank-quasi.tldr: A sparse-plus-low-rank Hessian approximation improves quasi-Newton optimization for entropy-regularized optimal transport, supported by convergence analysis and numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general forecasting model around two complementary needs: finding representations shared across different time-series domains and retaining information specific to each domain. Both matter when pretraining on heterogeneous datasets and transferring to new prediction settings. The approach focuses on representation design and adaptation as routes to better generalization.

For shared representations, the authors introduce Decomposed Frequency Learning. This pretraining task masks and reconstructs frequency-based information to separate semantic content that is coupled together in the original series. For domain-specific information, they introduce the Time Series Register, which captures representations during pretraining that help the model adapt to downstream tasks.

The two components address how a model can share knowledge while remaining responsive to differences between forecasting settings. On seven real-world benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art forecasting performance and strong few-shot and zero-shot capabilities. These findings support treating cross-domain commonality and domain-specific adaptation as distinct, jointly useful parts of a general time-series forecasting model.
icml-2025-towards-a-general-time-series-.tldr: Frequency-based pretraining and a domain-specific register combine shared time-series representations with adaptive transfer for general forecasting.

paragraphs: SQGEF addresses geographical forecasting when individual entities have limited historical observations. Separate studies may measure different regions, variables, and periods, leaving each dataset incomplete in its own way. The paper proposes combining their complementary information to learn representations of the underlying geographical system.

The framework uses a new data structure called a Segment Quadtree to accommodate entities at different spatial granularities. It integrates datasets with varying target entities, observation variables, and time spans into unified geographical representations. Alongside interactions at multiple levels in grid data, it captures nested relationships and human-defined boundaries, allowing several forms of geographical organization to inform the representation.

A central capability is representing entities that were absent during training. Experiments on real-world datasets show that SQGEF can represent these unseen entities effectively and improve the performance of various models. The contribution is a way to reuse fragmented geographical observations across spatial scales, helping forecasting models draw on more than the limited history available for any single entity.
icml-2025-unifying-knowledge-from-divers.tldr: SQGEF combines heterogeneous geographical datasets into representations across spatial scales, improving forecasting and supporting entities unseen during training.
